Need to search first.Now fetch full pages.I've written notes on all 12 verses, but some sections are thin. The research tool stopped working partway through, so I couldn't open most pages in full. These notes come only from the parts of pages that the searches returned. Here's what's missing:
- **Not reached at all:** NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, Wesley, the Lutheran, Pentecostal and Orthodox sites, and Catholic material other than Augustine.
- **Found nothing on:** prosperity or word-of-faith teaching on this psalm.
- **Not seen in full:** Enduring Word and Spurgeon's *Treasury of David*.
- **Unlabelled excerpts:** On the BibleHub pages that collect many commentaries, some excerpts didn't show the author's name. I've marked those "unnamed" rather than guessing who wrote them.

**Overview**
- Enduring Word says the psalm celebrates a great victory, probably God's defeat of the Assyrian king Sennacherib (Isaiah 37:36). On that view, the "Asaph" of the title is a later Asaph, or a literal or spiritual descendant of the first one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-76/
- The Pulpit Commentary says scholars of all schools agree the rescue was from Sennacherib. So "Asaph" means the group of Levites named after him, not the man himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-76.html
- Constable calls it a victory hymn that may not refer to any one battle. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-76.html
- Spurgeon calls it a joyful war song. Psalm 75 sang of victories still to come; this psalm sings of victories already won. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps076.cfm

**v. 1**
- **The title:** An unnamed commentator says Asaph either wrote it himself, or David or another prophet wrote it and gave it to Asaph or his descendants. The *Commentary Critical and Explanatory* (JFB) says this psalm celebrates the rescue that Psalm 75 looked forward to. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-1.htm
- **Pulpit:** "Known" means made known again by the recent rescue. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-1.htm
- **Barnes:** God shows his character most clearly among his own people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-1.htm
- **Gill:** He reads "name" in terms of Christ, as great Saviour, Priest, Prophet and King. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-1.htm
- **When was it written? The sources disagree:**
  - JFB and an unnamed commentator say the northern kingdom had already fallen, so "Israel" here simply means Judah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-76.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-1.htm
  - Utley (bible.org) says naming both Judah and Israel points to the time of the two kingdoms. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-76
- **Augustine (Catholic and Orthodox heritage):** Some Jews used this verse to claim God was known only to them. Augustine answers that God is truly known in "Judaea," if you understand what Judaea really is. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801076.htm

**v. 2**
- **Gill:** Salem is Jerusalem, where the tabernacle and later the temple stood. He also applies it to Christ's human body as the true tabernacle, and to the church. He notes that the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) translates "Salem" as "in peace." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-2.html
- **Pulpit:** The word for "tent" can mean a lion's den (compare Jeremiah 25:38). God is pictured as a lion springing from Zion on the enemy. Readers should remember God is everywhere and not shut him into one place. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-76.html
- BibleHub's study page links Salem to Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:1–2). https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/76.htm
- In the "Explanatory Notes" section of Spurgeon's *Treasury*, a writer says God steers world events for Zion's good. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps076.cfm
- **Augustine:** God's place is "in peace," and you make room for him in your heart by confessing your sins. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801076.htm

**v. 3**
- **Pulpit and Coffman:** "There" places the defeat at or near Jerusalem, where Sennacherib's army was destroyed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-1.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-76.html
- **JFB:** Listing "battle" last means the whole war ended at one stroke (compare Psalm 46:9). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-76.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Even a favoured people still faced real danger. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-5.html
- **Utley:** This is "holy war" language; Israel trusted God and didn't need weapons. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-76

**v. 4**
- **Gill:** The verse is about God, or Christ, not Zion. The "mountains of prey" are earthly kingdoms won by violence, like mountains where lions hunt, and Christ is greater than all of them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-4.html
- **Pulpit, on the translation:** It lists several readings: the hills where the enemy camped, and the Prayer Book's "hills of the robbers." It prefers "coming down from the mountains of prey," picturing the lion returning in triumph. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-76.html
- **Constable:** "Resplendent" pictures God giving off light. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-76.html
- BibleHub links the verse to Habakkuk 3:4. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/76.htm

**v. 5**
- **Clarke:** The "valiant" are the boasting Rabshakeh (the Assyrian commander) and his master Sennacherib. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-5.html
- **Calvin:** The enemy lost the courage they bragged about; neither mind nor body could do its job. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-5.html
- **Coffman:** The Septuagint reads "found nothing in their hands." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-5.html
- **Matthew Henry:** The strong couldn't even "find their hands" to save themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_076.cfm
- **Utley:** "Stouthearted" suggests a stubborn attitude against God. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-76

**v. 6**
- **Spurgeon:** Israel especially feared horses and chariots, so their sudden silence is a special cause for joy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps076.cfm
- **Coffman:** "Chariot" stands for the driver. Matthew Henry says the same: the chariots "sleep" because their drivers do. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-5.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_076.cfm
- **Utley:** God's "rebuke" is his powerful voice, a way of speaking of his will at work in the world. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-76
- "Horse and rider" echoes the Red Sea song (Exodus 15). https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/76.htm
- **Pulpit Homiletics:** God's rebukes are sometimes actions, such as the night attack on Assyria or Herod's illness. They still answer "presumptuous sins" today. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/76.htm

**v. 7**
- **Pulpit Homiletics:** Scripture describes God's anger in human terms, but we must remove the sin from the picture. God's anger is like a judge's response to public wrong, not personal hatred. God should be feared more for his holiness and love than for his raw power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/76.htm
- **Pulpit (Spanish edition):** God's mercy deepens holy fear rather than removing it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-1.html
- **Utley:** Some translations group v. 7 with vv. 8–10. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-76

**v. 8**
- **Benson:** The judgment came through an angel sent from heaven, and other nations were afraid to invade Israel afterwards. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-8.htm
- **Barnes:** The defeat was clearly God's own act. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-8.htm
- **Pulpit:** God spoke "with a voice of thunder" to the nations (2 Chronicles 32:23). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-8.htm
- **Gill:** He offers several readings: possible thunder or an earthquake at the time; God's coming judgments on anti-Christian powers; and the Last Judgment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-8.htm
- **Coffman, quoting Kidner:** This points ahead to God's final blow against evil everywhere (Revelation 6:12–17). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-8.html
- **Constable:** Perhaps it pictures the calm before a storm. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/76-8.html

**v. 9**
- **Pulpit:** The "lowly" are those who, like King Hezekiah, stayed faithful to God in hopeless trouble. It also includes other nations oppressed by Assyria. "With God judgment is salvation," like the pillar of cloud: dark to Egypt, light to Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-76.html
- **Coffman, quoting Yates:** Israel represents all oppressed peoples. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-76.html
- **Utley:** The humble are those who revere God. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-76

**v. 10** (the hardest verse)
- **Ellicott:** The Hebrew "as it stands is unintelligible," so he proposes a small correction to the text. "The survivors of wrath" would then mean Israelites who escaped, holding a festival like the one first promised to Pharaoh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-10.htm
- **Pulpit:** The meaning is uncertain. Quoting Jennings and Lowe, it says Assyria's hostility only made God's power more widely known, and the small group of survivors could do nothing. It cites the Septuagint as "the remainder of wrath shall keep a feast to thee." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-76.html
- **Benson:** The enemy's rage and boasting end up serving God's glory. "Restrain" means God blocks their later plans. Or, translating "gird," God wears their wrath like a winner wears captured spoils. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-10.htm
- **An unnamed commentator on the same page:** God uses people's wrath (Judas, Sennacherib, the persecutors of the church) for his purposes, but that does not excuse it; people are judged for their own deeds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-10.htm
- **Another unnamed commentator there:** Several meanings are possible, including God's wrath against his people, which Christ bore for them. Sennacherib was kept from returning by his sudden death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-10.htm
- **Matthew Henry and the *Biblical Illustrator*:** God sets limits to human rage, as he does to the sea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/76-10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-76.html
- **Pulpit Homiletics (Conway):** God turns evil to good. Examples include the Fall leading to redemption, the cross, persecution spreading the church, and "the corruption of the Church led to the Reformation." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/76.htm

**v. 11**
- **Pulpit:** Vows today are like our solemn resolutions: easy to make and easy to neglect. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-76.html
- **Matthew Henry:** God doesn't need our gifts. Our prayers, our praise and above all our hearts are the gifts to bring. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_076.cfm
- **Enduring Word:** Honour God with more than vows; bring him your first and best. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-76/
- **Constable:** God's people should keep their vows. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-76.html
- **Precept Austin:** The Hebrew word for "fulfill" means "pay back." https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_47-8
- **Augustine:** The psalm doesn't say "don't vow" but "vow and pay." Every believer should vow to believe, to hope for eternal life and to live a godly life. God's help completes what we vow. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801076.htm

**v. 12**
- **Pulpit:** "Spirit" here means life. God cuts princes off in their prime, as a gardener cuts grapes (Isaiah 18:5), and kings too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-76.html
- **Matthew Henry:** God removes it as easily as slipping a flower from its stem. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_076.cfm
- **JFB:** This means Rabshakeh and the other princes were actually killed, not just driven off. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-76.html
- **Constable:** Leaders should submit to God rather than rebel. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-76.html

**Differences between traditions:** The commentators I could read, from Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon), Reformed (Calvin) and other backgrounds, didn't really disagree by denomination. The real split is in method:
- Some read the psalm historically, about Sennacherib (Pulpit, Barnes, Benson).
- Gill reads it about Christ and the end times.
- Augustine reads it about the inner life of each believer.

The main debated point is how to translate and read v. 10, set out above.
